title: Female Nervous System Anatomy: Brain, Cord & Pelvis Map
description: Study female nervous system anatomy across the brain, spinal cord, limb plexuses, uterovaginal autonomic plexuses, and somatic pudendal perineal nerve map.
h1: Female Nervous System Anatomy: Whole-Body Tracts and Pelvic Nerves
blurb: Whole-body central and peripheral nerve pathways on the female figure, highlighting limb plexuses alongside uterovaginal autonomic and pudendal pelvic nerves.
lead: From cerebral motor pathways down to the uterovaginal plexus and pudendal branches of the pelvis, the female nervous system integrates whole-body and reproductive signaling. In this illustrated guide to female nervous system anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including brain, spinal cord, cervical plexus, brachial plexus—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: From cerebral motor pathways down to the uterovaginal plexus and pudendal branches of the pelvis, the female nervous system integrates whole-body and reproductive signaling. This female figure orients the shared brain, spinal and peripheral nerve plan. The additional study structures focus on nerves to the uterus, vagina, clitoris and vulva. Deep pelvic branches are not individually depicted on the full-body image. Within the human body, the nervous system — female (Systema nervosum (femina)) is situated in female body, anterior, receives arterial perfusion via as overview, and is innervated by as overview.

Structurally, the brain (Encephalon) comprises cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem inside the cranial vault. Physiologically, the brain governs integration, consciousness, motor planning and autonomic control. Structurally, the spinal cord (Medulla spinalis) comprises 31-segment cord from foramen magnum to L1–L2. Physiologically, the spinal cord governs two-way tracts plus segmental reflex circuits. Structurally, the cervical plexus (Plexus cervicalis (C1–C4)) comprises nerve network in the posterior triangle of the neck. Physiologically, the cervical plexus governs neck muscles and skin; phrenic nerve to diaphragm. Structurally, the brachial plexus (Plexus brachialis (C5–T1)) comprises roots-trunks-divisions-cords-branches behind the clavicle. Physiologically, the brachial plexus governs all motor and sensory supply of the upper limb. Structurally, the intercostal nerves (Nn. intercostales (T1–T11)) comprises ventral rami running in subcostal grooves. Physiologically, the intercostal nerves governs chest-wall muscles and segmental skin band. Structurally, the lumbar plexus (Plexus lumbalis (L1–L4)) comprises network within psoas major. Physiologically, the lumbar plexus governs anterior thigh and medial leg supply.

Clinically, regarding the brain, head injury scales from concussion to diffuse axonal injury. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the spinal cord, cord transection level predicts deficit pattern precisely. In clinical pathology involving the cervical plexus, c3-4-5 keeps the diaphragm alive — injury above C4 stops breathing. Medical evaluation of the brachial plexus also notes that erb's palsy (C5-6) from birth traction: waiter's-tip hand.

questions.question: Is the female nervous system built differently from the male nervous system?
questions.answer: The central and most peripheral pathways share the same basic organization. A female-focused pelvic view discusses branches serving the uterus, vagina, clitoris and vulva without implying a separate female brain or spinal cord. Structurally, the uterovaginal plexus comprises pelvic autonomic network associated with the cervix and upper vagina. Physiologically, the uterovaginal plexus distributes fibers toward the uterus, cervix and upper vagina.

questions.question: What carries sensation from the clitoral glans?
questions.answer: The dorsal nerve of the clitoris, a terminal branch of the pudendal nerve, conveys much of the somatic sensation. Autonomic nerves influence erectile tissues but should not be confused with that sensory pathway. Structurally, the dorsal nerve of clitoris comprises terminal sensory branch of the pudendal nerve runs toward the clitoral glans. Physiologically, the dorsal nerve of clitoris governs conveys much of the clitoral somatic sensation.

questions.question: Which nerves supply the vulva and lower vagina?
questions.answer: Pudendal branches supply much of the posterior vulva and lower vaginal region. The anterior labia also receive contributions from ilioinguinal and genitofemoral branches, so a single nerve label cannot cover the entire area. Structurally, the posterior labial nerves comprises cutaneous branches of the pudendal perineal nerve enter the posterior labial region. Physiologically, the posterior labial nerves supply sensation to posterior vulvar skin.

questions.question: What is the uterovaginal plexus?
questions.answer: It is an autonomic network associated with the cervix and upper vagina that carries branches toward the uterus and upper vagina. It is anatomically distinct from the superficial pudendal branches of the perineum. The vaginal autonomic branches branches from the pelvic plexus reach the upper vaginal wall. Physiologically, the vaginal autonomic branches carry autonomic innervation and visceral sensory pathways.

questions.question: Does the full-body female nerve plate identify tiny pelvic branches?
questions.answer: No. The full-body plate is for orientation to larger pathways. The pudendal nerve is paired somatic S2–S4 nerve passes through the pudendal canal toward the perineum. Physiologically, the pudendal nerve supplies external genital and perineal sensation plus motor branches to sphincters.
